primary_meaning: In Christian teaching and biblical interpretation, the bow is most commonly read as a symbol of military power, strength, and warfare — and by extension of God's judgment when God is depicted bending or drawing his bow against the wicked. Correspondingly, the breaking or removal of the bow symbolizes the end of war, the humbling of human might, and the peace God establishes.
primary_basis: Psalm 46:9 (God breaks the bow and shatters the spear, making wars cease)
Psalm 7:12-13 (God bends his bow against the unrepentant, an image of divine judgment)
Hosea 1:5 and 2:18 (breaking the bow of Israel; abolishing the bow and sword from the land)
Zechariah 9:10 (the battle bow cut off; the messianic king speaks peace to the nations)
Jeremiah 49:35 (breaking the bow of Elam, the mainstay of their might)
Genesis 49:24 (Joseph's bow remained steady — bow as personal strength)
1 Samuel 2:4 (the bows of the mighty are broken — reversal of human power)
Lamentations 2:4 and Habakkuk 3:9 (God's bow as instrument of judgment)

alternatives.meaning: The bow as the rainbow of Genesis 9 (Hebrew qeshet, the same word as the war-bow), interpreted as the sign of God's covenant with Noah and all creation — divine mercy, faithfulness, and the promise never again to destroy the earth by flood. Many interpreters explicitly connect the two senses, reading the rainbow as God's war-bow hung up or pointed away from the earth, signifying that God has set aside hostility.
basis: Ezekiel 1:28 (the bow in the cloud surrounding God's glory)
Revelation 4:3 and 10:1 (rainbow around the throne and the mighty angel)

alternatives.meaning: The bow of the rider on the white horse in Revelation 6:2 as a symbol of conquest — read by some as Christ or the victorious gospel, and by others (more commonly in modern interpretation) as the Antichrist or a counterfeit conqueror unleashing war.
The 'deceitful' or 'slack' bow as an image of unfaithfulness and unreliability — Israel turning aside like a treacherous bow that misses its mark.
The bow (with arrows/children) as an image of family strength and blessing — the warrior whose quiver is full, sometimes extended to the bow as the instrument by which children are 'sent forth.'
The bow as covenant loyalty or personal devotion in the Jonathan narratives (Jonathan giving David his bow; the 'Song of the Bow'), read as friendship and covenant fidelity.

notes: The consensus is bifurcated because 'bow' in Scripture covers two distinct referents sharing one Hebrew word (qeshet): the war-bow (power, warfare, judgment, and its breaking as peace) and the rainbow (covenant mercy, Genesis 9). Both readings are firmly established in Christian interpretation; which one is 'primary' depends on which referent the interpreter has in view. The weapon sense dominates by frequency of biblical occurrence, while the Genesis 9 covenant-rainbow reading is arguably the single most prominent symbolic use in popular Christian teaching. The interpretive tradition linking the two — the rainbow as God's unstrung or reversed war-bow — appears in both Jewish and Christian commentary and is widely cited, though not universally accepted. Confidence is medium because of this dual referent rather than any lack of established interpretation.
